doc.title: Oliver Nelson Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 10, 2020

title: Father's training and the range Hollywood demanded
summary: Early gig stories, then his father's path from streetcar driver to Marines, Washington University and a Ph.D. in composition, which let him write anything for Hollywood.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: Real early on in life. I’ve got a ton of stories to tell you about gigs and Dad and all that kind of stuff. And I’ve probably seen more than most because I’ve seen great players scuffle to play this music. You know but he just sets it down there and you’ve just got to count this stuff off and go, and it doesn’t necessarily go all the time the way you actually want it to go. And then his career was really interesting too because he drove a streetcar in St. Louis for a while, but he always wanted to be into music so eventually he got in the Marines and learned music there and went back to Washington University and studied with a guy named Robert Wykes who was also a flautist, studied with Joseph Mariano at Eastman, but he also got his Ph.D. in composition. So Dad really studied. And that was one of the big differences between him and a lot of jazz guys. He could write anything. [Inaudible] Hollywood really prepared him because he had to write anything at any time for any producer based upon what he was working on at the time.

That came to mind today because I was listening to some of his themes and you went from “The Six Million Dollar Man” with all these sirens and all this, and then to “The Virginian.” Like all of a sudden we’re going back like a hundred years and it’s sort of frontiery, and that’s just so admirable.
